entries.title: How HP Is Building an AI-Ready CDP with Databricks CustomerLake
entries.summary: At Data + AI Summit 2026, Luis Alonso, Global Head of Data Strategy & Engineering...
entries.content:
HP modernized its marketing data foundation with Databricks CustomerLake and Genie, accelerating audience creation to 2 hours instead of 2-3 months, reducing CDP costs by up to 40%, and expanding available marketing data by 90%.

by Katy Yuan

  • HP became audience-ready in 2 hours instead of 2 to 3 months. With Databricks CustomerLake, HP configured governed data models and published attributes directly on its existing Databricks foundation, dramatically accelerating audience creation.
  • HP estimates up to 40% lower CDP total cost of ownership. Consolidating CDP capabilities with CustomerLake could reduce HP’s TCO by up to 40% compared with its former composable CDP approach.
  • HP expanded its marketing context with 90% net-new signals. HP unified media, brand, intent and technographic data in its Marketing Lakehouse, expanded intent-data ingestion from 75 to approximately 20,000 topics, and reduced comparable governed data-sharing timelines from three months to 48 hours.

At Data + AI Summit 2026, Luis Alonso, Global Head of Data Strategy & Engineering for MarTech & AI Enablement at HP, shared how the company is building an AI-ready go-to-market data foundation on Databricks.

HP has spent extensive time and effort unifying customer data and third-party signals in their Marketing Lakehouse, and now Genie and CustomerLake make that trusted context available to marketers making daily decisions about audiences, channels, and customer journeys.

HP’s early work highlights three ways this approach can reduce costs, expand available customer context, and accelerate activation:

  • 40% lower CDP total cost of ownership: HP estimates that consolidating CDP capabilities with CustomerLake could reduce total cost of ownership by up to 40% compared to its former Composable CDP approach.
  • 90% net-new marketing signals: HP expanded the data available for marketing with 90% net-new signals across media, brand, intent, and technographic sources.
  • Audience-ready in two hours: In the first session of using CustomerLake, HP configured data models, published attributes, and became ready to build audiences — a process that could’ve taken 2-3 months with a traditional CDP.

For HP, a CDP isn't one product or a narrow set of activation features. It's a collection of capabilities built around the needs of the business:

  • First- and third-party data strategy
  • Account profiling and clustering
  • Identity and buying-group intelligence
  • Audience segmentation and activation
  • Closed-loop measurement
  • Always-on automation and self-service

As HP consolidated more governed data and business logic on Databricks, maintaining a separate CDP increasingly meant duplicating pipelines, data and operational overhead. Composable architectures reduced some data movement, but the activation layer still lacked the business definitions, context, and governance already available in the data platform.

That context is essential for self-service analytics and AI agents. Without it, an agent may be able to access data but still lack the definitions, relationships, metrics and governance needed to use it correctly.

HP's broader data transformation consolidated hundreds of data lakes and repositories into a small number of Databricks lakehouses. The company uses central standards with federated execution, allowing domain experts to retain ownership and stewardship while sharing governed data products across the business.

This gave marketing governed access to previously fragmented sources, including media performance, market-share, technographic and intent data, along with propensity models.

The change has materially changed how HP teams work together.

Alonso described a 2024 request to share data with a sales partner that required three months, roughly 15 email exchanges and three escalations, without a reliable outcome. Today, a comparable request can result in a governed Delta Sharing asset within 48 hours.

That improvement gives marketing faster access to the data it needs for planning, targeting, reporting and measurement, while preserving domain ownership and governance.

Creating a strong technical foundation doesn't automatically make data usable for marketers. The next step is enabling executives, marketing users, media teams and analysts to use that foundation without relying on engineering for every question or task.

HP is using AI/BI Genie and agent-based capabilities to help bridge that gap across three layers of work:

  • Decision-making and planning for executives and business teams
  • Insight generation and activation for marketers, analysts and data scientists
  • Building and scaling for engineering teams

Business context is a core part of that strategy. HP is developing semantic layers that help Genie understand what the company's data means, including domains, metric views, instructions and reusable skills.

For example, HP created a media metric view covering 26 dimensions and 10 measures. This centralizes definitions for media-spend and performance KPIs so dashboards, business users and AI systems can work from the same source of truth.

HP has also expanded its intent-data ingestion from 75 topics to approximately 20,000 topics. Genie Code helps the team plan how to cluster those signals at scale and use them for richer account profiles.

HP is also rethinking where identity resolution should live. Historically, companies often sent customer data to an external identity provider and kept the resulting identity layer outside their core data environment.

HP plans to bring identity signals back into its Databricks environment. That creates a governed foundation for measurement, audience activation and model improvement. Data can flow through the same identity service on its way to media platforms and on the return path, helping HP build a more complete view of performance and continuously improve its models.

Alonso noted that reaching even 10% of HP's consumer customer base through this consent-preserving approach could create a substantial new opportunity for the commercial business.

HP's early experience with CustomerLake illustrates the potential of bringing marketing capabilities directly to the governed data foundation.

Based on the team's prior CDP implementations, Alonso expected a long setup process involving extensive meetings, documentation, data-model configuration, and privacy and security reviews.

The initial experience was dramatically simpler.

“We had our data models in place, we had attributes published, and we were ready to build audiences — work that might have previously required two or three months to complete.”

Because CustomerLake is native to Databricks and Unity Catalog, HP's team could work directly with their schemas, tables, definitions, and governance, instead of recreating context in a separate platform.

The architecture also supports a significant B2C-to-B2B opportunity. HP has hundreds of millions of consumer customers, but a much smaller known population of business contacts. CustomerLake makes it possible for HP to work across both their B2C and B2B data models and systems in one environment through a shared identity layer. HP can also incorporate data from other platforms using Lakehouse Federation.

Across the go-to-market roadmap, HP is evaluating value in three areas:

  • Outcomes: Better insights, planning, activation, reporting and measurement
  • Productivity: Faster model development, audience creation and data access
  • TCO: Lower platform, licensing, integration and operational costs

HP’s work with Genie and CustomerLake suggests potential to address all three areas together. Their journey offers four practical takeaways for other enterprises modernizing their marketing stack:

  • Define the CDP around business needs. Start with the capabilities your stakeholders need rather than a rigid category definition or product checklist.
  • Build a governed Marketing Lakehouse. Data unification, quality, and access need to be in place before self-service and agents can work reliably.
  • Choose CDP capabilities closest to your data and AI. AI agents work best when customer context, business definitions, and activation capabilities operate on the same foundation, giving them the context to act accurately and safely at scale.
  • Measure outcomes, productivity, and TCO together. Faster activation, revenue impact, reduced engineering overhead, and lower platform costs are connected parts of the same transformation.

HP’s journey shows that modernizing marketing activation and applying AI at scale both depend on bringing data, intelligence, and action together on the same foundation. With CustomerLake and Genie on its governed Marketing Lakehouse, HP is giving marketers and agents direct access to trusted context without recreating it across disconnected systems. The early results include becoming audience-ready in two hours instead of months, with the potential to reduce CDP TCO by up to 40%. Together, these gains lay the foundation for faster, more intelligent and more personalized customer engagement at scale.

entries.title: What makes a catalog open? Unity Catalog Advances the Open Lakehouse
entries.summary: While almost every platform now supports open formats, what makes a catalog truly...
entries.content:
Unity Catalog keeps your data in storage you own, readable and writable from external engines, and now free to move between catalogs without copying data.

  • Customer-owned storage: Unlike other platforms with native tables in managed storage, Unity Catalog managed tables in customer-owned storage allow portability without data copy.
  • Unity Catalog is the most open catalog: As the first catalog to support the Apache Iceberg REST catalog spec for REGISTER and UNREGISTER, Unity Catalog allows you to move tables between catalogs without data duplication.
  • Best features available on tables you own: Open catalogs like Unity Catalog deliver all advanced table features on tables in your storage, not only on tables a provider stores for you.

While almost every platform now supports open formats, what makes a catalog truly open? An open catalog keeps your data in storage you own, gives you the best features there, and supports data portability: the ability to move your tables to another catalog while keeping the data in place. Portability is a core tenet of an open lakehouse, and it’s where most catalogs fall short.

As the first catalog to support both REGISTER and UNREGISTER from the Apache Iceberg™ REST catalog spec, Unity Catalog in Databricks' Open Lakehouse expands what an open catalog means: your tables can move existing Iceberg tables in or out without any data movement. Databricks contributed UNREGISTER to the Iceberg REST catalog spec, making this an open standard. Read Unlocking Data Portability.

This post walks through the three requirements of an open catalog, how Unity Catalog meets each one, and compares what happens to the same Iceberg table on different platforms.

How open a lakehouse is comes down to the catalog. Many providers still use a proprietary format for the primary table type in their catalog, so formats are important to pay attention to. Beyond this however, an open catalog must also meet three requirements:

Open catalog requirement What it means What happens without it
1. Storage you own Tables live in customer-owned storage rather than managed storage (i.e. “provider-controlled storage”) The bucket sits in the provider's cloud account, not yours. Storage is billed through the provider, so you pay storage “rent”, plus the provider will charge you for moving data out.
2. Best features Included Automatic optimizations and all advanced table features work on tables in customer-owned storage, not only those in provider-controlled storage

Teams move tables into provider-controlled storage to get

features the customer-owned option lacks. From then on, the provider's roadmap decides what you can do with your data.
3. Free to Move without Copy Tables can enter and leave the catalog using REGISTER and UNREGISTER, with data staying in place

Changing catalogs means exporting and rewriting every

table, to move it out of provider-controlled storage.

Most data platforms support open table formats like Apache Iceberg. However, when those tables live in buckets that belong to the provider, your tables are no longer open. That makes the format open in name only: you can't see the files in your own cloud account, storage is billed through the provider, and leaving means copying every table out first.

Unity Catalog takes the opposite approach. In Databricks, "managed" describes who maintains a table, not who owns its storage. The catalog handles optimization, maintenance, and upgrades, while the files stay in a cloud storage account you own, not in the proprietary storage other platforms often call "managed storage." In Databricks, 99% of UC managed tables are in customer-owned storage. On platforms built around provider-controlled storage, it’s the opposite: nearly all of their tables live in storage that the provider controls and are locked in a proprietary format by default. The difference shows up the day you decide to leave a catalog.

Owning your storage only matters if the catalog treats those tables as first-class. Some platforms offer a customer-owned storage option, but reserve their best capabilities for tables in managed storage they control, creating an illusion of openness. The open path exists, but it comes with fewer features, so most tables would end up in provider managed storage anyway.

With Unity Catalog managed tables, the best features are supported for customer-owned storage (“bring your own storage”) path, whereas other platforms have limitations:

  • Fail-safe data protection. Snowflake and other platforms reserve fail-safe recovery for tables in their own storage. By contrast, Unity Catalog managed tables in customer-owned storage support data recovery: you can query earlier versions or restore dropped tables for up to 30 days.
  • Automatic optimizations. In Snowflake, data compaction is costlier in provider-controlled storage. For other platforms, table maintenance and V-order apply to tables stored in customer-owned storage, rather than data reached through shortcuts. Databricks’ Predictive Optimization Runs on Unity Catalog managed tables in both Delta and Iceberg formats in customer-owned storage.
  • Storage costs. Snowflake doesn't delete orphaned files from Iceberg tables in your own bucket, such as files left behind by failed writes, which means you keep paying for files no table uses. On Unity Catalog managed tables on the other hand, Predictive Optimization removes unreferenced files from your bucket automatically, saving you money.
Unity Catalog managed tables' automatic optimizations saved us over $1 million annually in storage costs while eliminating the need for tedious manual effort on a daily basis. —Abhinav Raghuvanshi, Associate Director of Data Engineering, Zepto

The most important test for whether a catalog is open is portability: whether you can leave the catalog easily at any time by moving tables between catalogs without having to copy out data.

Until recently, the ecosystem didn’t have a standard way to release a table from a catalog's management. Therefore, Databricks contributed UNREGISTER to the Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification which gives customers the freedom to leave without having to copy, move or rewrite any data files.

In Unity Catalog, REGISTER and UNREGISTER work as a pair:

  • UNREGISTER removes a table from Unity Catalog and returns the table's latest metadata location, the exact pointer the next catalog needs to take over commits.
  • REGISTER attaches that metadata location to a new catalog, which writes a single record linking the table name to its metadata.

This is made possible because Unity Catalog managed tables reside in storage that you own. Unregistering isn’t possible with provider controlled storage since the exit API can’t hand you a pointer to files that you can't take with you.

Unity Catalog managed tables are fully portable and open with no lock-in: you retain control of your own data.

To get started in Databricks, reach out to your account team to get access to REGISTER and UNREGISTER (in Private Preview). With REGISTER and UNREGISTER, your Iceberg tables move to Unity Catalog with zero data copy into Databricks, stay fully open in your own storage, and gain all the benefits of Unity Catalog and Predictive Optimization:

To learn more, read Unlocking Data Portability. See Unity Catalog managed tables documentation for more details on how to use Unity Catalog managed tables, which exist in customer-owned storage.

In the future, we plan to support converting foreign tables or external tables to Databricks to managed tables using SET MANAGED IN PLACE. This would allow you to keep the same customer-defined storage path as before and does not require any data movement.

Yes. Unity Catalog is open source and meets three requirements of an open catalog. Its managed tables, in Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake, live in a cloud storage account you own, get the full feature set there, and can move to another catalog without copying data through REGISTER and UNREGISTER. Most importantly, Unity Catalog managed tables are in customer-owned storage, so UNREGISTER in Databricks provides catalog portability without data movement on the Unity Catalog side. Read and write access to manage tables is also supported, using Unity Catalog and Iceberg REST Catalog Open APIs.

Not on its own. An Iceberg table in provider-controlled storage can be as hard to move as a proprietary table, and an Iceberg table in your own storage may get fewer features. Avoiding lock-in also requires storage you own, full features on those tables, and a catalog that supports a clean, no-copy handoff.

In Unity Catalog, "managed" describes who maintains a table, not who owns its storage. Unity Catalog managed tables are optimized and maintained by the catalog, and their files live in a cloud storage account you own. On some other platforms, "managed storage" means storage the provider owns and controls, not just optimizes.

Yes. With UNREGISTER, you can remove a table from Unity Catalog and register it in another Iceberg REST catalog, without copying data files.

In Unity Catalog, "managed" describes who maintains a table, not who owns its storage. Unity Catalog managed tables are optimized and maintained by the catalog, but their files live in a cloud storage account you own. On some other platforms, "managed storage" means storage the provider owns and often keeps in proprietary table formats.

Foreign Iceberg tables are read-only in Databricks because another catalog owns their commits, which prevents two catalogs from writing to the same table. To have Unity Catalog manage the table in customer-owned storage, register it in Unity Catalog with REGISTER. You can also convert foreign tables to Unity Catalog managed tables in customer-owned storage using SET MANAGED.

entries.title: How to get the most out of running dbt on Databricks
entries.summary: Tens of thousands of organizations rely on dbt for data transformation. Where you...
entries.content:
Make dbt pipelines on Databricks cheaper, faster and simpler to operate.

by Srilekha Dornadula and Luís Cabral

  • Avoid stitching separate tools together and keep the whole pipeline in one dbt project on Databricks, from streaming ingestion through governed metric definitions
  • Orchestrate dbt natively in Lakeflow Jobs without the need for an external orchestrator.
  • Define governance in the dbt project itself, so access rules are enforced by Unity Catalog straight from your project configs.

Tens of thousands of organizations rely on dbt for data transformation. Where you run it shapes everything: how much it costs to run your dbt pipelines, how fast they ship, and how much operational work they carry. Running dbt on Databricks gives your dbt workloads an open platform and a unified pipeline.

Over 3000 organizations run dbt on Databricks, and most teams could be getting a lot more out of it. This blog highlights the practices that make dbt pipelines cheaper, faster, and simpler to operate on Databricks.

dbt bills climb from work you don't need to repeat. Full rebuilds recompute data that hasn't changed, keeping queries fast takes manual-tuning, and when the bill spikes there's no clear attribution back to the dbt models that caused it. Adopt the practices in this section and your pipelines will:

  • Rebuild only the data that actually changed
  • Stay fast without you choosing or reworking partition keys
  • Run table maintenance automatically without post-hooks
  • race every dollar of spend to a specific model

Full table rebuilds are the largest avoidable cost in most dbt projects. When only a small fraction of the data changes between runs, recomputing the entire table wastes your compute and increases your bill. dbt's incremental strategies, all supported on dbt-databricks, let each model process only new data, and the right choice depends on how your data actually arrives.

Strategy

Use it when

append

Rows are only ever inserted, never updated

merge

The same key can arrive more than once and needs upserting (slowly changing dimensions, dedupe, late-arriving updates)

replace_where

(dbt-databricks specific)

The model re-derives a narrow time window each run, such as the last few days of activity

insert_overwrite

Your query returns whole partitions

delete+insert

(dbt-databricks specific)

You want records replaced by key, without column-level update logic

microbatch

Time-series data with an event_time column and structured backfill needs

Most projects default to 

merge
when a narrower strategy would do. If you can describe the changed data with a predicate, 
replace_where
does less work than a 
merge
that has to scan the target to find matches. If you can't, 
incremental_predicates
on the 
merge
narrows that scan considerably.

Every strategy above is a decision you make and have to maintain. The next practice lets the platform take care of this for you.

Materialized views automate incrementalization. You can define the model as plain SQL, and Databricks tracks which underlying data has changed and refreshes only the affected results. On dbt-databricks, a materialized view is a native materialization, so this is a one-line config change:

Materialized views fit best at the serving layer: aggregations over frequently changing sources, especially the expensive ones that back dashboards and need to stay fresh. In our TPC-DI benchmark, switching full recomputes to materialized views at the serving layer delivered 17x speedup.

Choosing partition keys, reworking them when query patterns change, and scheduling 

OPTIMIZE
, 
VACUUM
, and 
ANALYZE
in post-hooks all take engineering time. 

Predictive Optimization runs 

OPTIMIZE
, 
VACUUM
, and statistics collection on managed tables automatically, choosing what to run and when based on how each table is queried. Enable it once at the catalog or schema level, and the post-hooks that dbt projects usually accumulate for table maintenance can be retired. 

For data layout, Liquid Clustering replaces partition design with a self-tuning layout. It organizes data based on how the table is actually queried, sidesteps the small-file explosion that over-partitioned tables hit, and adapts as query patterns drift. Or let Databricks choose and adjust them from query history with automatic Liquid Clustering (

CLUSTER BY AUTO
), powered by Predictive Optimization. A single project-level config clusters every new table the project builds.

Both features are designed as one-time decisions. With Automatic upgrades, Unity Catalog managed tables keep picking up new optimizations as Databricks ships them.

At the end of the quarter, finance asks why the warehouse bill went up. In most setups nobody can answer, because a query in the usage data carries no connection to the dbt model that issued it.

Query tags make the connection automatic. Every query dbt runs on Databricks is automatically stamped with the model name, dbt version, and materialization type. Add your own DIY custom tags for the dimensions your organization budgets by:

The tags surface in system.query.history, and joining against system.billing.usage attributes serverless warehouse spend to any grouping the tags support: cost by model, by team, by domain, by materialization. You can see exactly which models cost the most.

A typical dbt setup leans on a stack of other tools: a separate system to ingest the data, an external orchestrator to run the project, BI tools that each redefine the same metrics, and governance that lives outside your dbt project. Each is one more thing to maintain and one more place for things to drift. Adopt the practices in this section and one dbt project will:

  • Ingest data directly into the project
  • Run and deploy from Databricks, without a third-party orchestrator to maintain
  • Serve one governed metric definition to every tool
  • Carry its own governance rules, versioned alongside your dbt models

Ingestion is the part of the pipeline that has traditionally lived outside dbt, resulting in a split architecture with no single lineage overview. The streaming_table materialization removes that split. A dbt model materialized as a streaming table incrementally picks up new files or events as they arrive, so ingestion becomes just another model in the DAG.

From there the rest of the pipeline (silver and gold models) can reference the streaming table with 

ref()
, tests and documentation apply to every layer, and lineage covers the whole path from raw files to the final mart.

Every BI tool, agent, or other consumer of data builds their own definitions of metrics, which leads to confusion and disagreement among stakeholders. A metric view moves the definition into one governed place: you declare the measures and dimensions once, and every consumer queries the same logic.

dbt-databricks exposes metric views as a native materialization type, so the definition lives in your dbt project, versioned and reviewed like any other model. 

Users can pick their own groupings at query time with the 

MEASURE()
function, so the same definition serves the SQL editor, BI dashboards, notebooks, and Genie.

A dbt run is rarely the whole pipeline. When upstream and downstream steps live in different tools, the overhead adds up: additional tools to manage, pay for, and secure, with scattered lineage.

Lakeflow Jobs collapses that into one Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with dbt as a native task. An ingestion task feeds the dbt task and downstream tasks trigger on completion, with dependencies enforced by the platform. The operational layer comes built in with scheduling, automatic retries, run history, and alerts, with no additional infrastructure to maintain. Jobs supports dbt Core and dbt Platform, and support for dbt Core v2.0 is on the way.

A job assembled by hand in the UI is hard to version, review, or reproduce. Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs) fix this by making the job definition part of the code repository. Lakeflow Job, its schedule, compute settings, and the dbt project, all declared in YAML and deployed as one package.

Deploying with 

--target dev
creates an isolated copy of the whole pipeline; 
--target prod
promotes it.

Not every model within a project needs to run on every schedule. Tag models by cadence in dbt YAML and give each cadence its own job that builds only the models carrying its tag. Moving a model from daily to hourly becomes a one-line change:

Governance is usually configured after your models run, separate from the dbt project that builds the data. Because governance sits outside your dbt project, it can drift out of sync with your dbt runs.

Define governance in the dbt project where the models already live. As project config, it ships with the code, gets reviewed like the code, and Unity Catalog enforces it on every query.

Tags, grants, and row and column-level protection all can be defined in project-wide config in dbt_project.yml. databricks_tags drives classification and policy, grants controls who can read the table, and row_filters and column_masks control what each user sees:

At scale, attribute-based access control (ABAC) removes the repetition. Define one policy on a governed tag and it applies the right row filters and column masks to every table carrying that tag, so a new model tagged 

pii
is covered the moment it builds. Reach for per-model filters and masks only when the logic is truly model-specific, like multi-tenant isolation.

The common thread across these practices is handing operational work to the platform: incremental processing, data layout, table maintenance, governance enforcement, and orchestration. What stays in your dbt project is your version-controlled and tested transformation logic. Pick the practice that addresses the pain your project has today and start there.

Join the 3000+ organizations already running dbt on Databricks. Get started with the dbt-databricks adapter.

entries.content:
Our New York R&D hub at 5 Bryant Park is doubling in size as our AI research, infrastructure and applications teams keep growing.

  • Databricks is doubling its New York City footprint at 5 Bryant Park to about 120,000 square feet across five floors. The space adds a dedicated Engineering and Research floor and an Executive Briefing Center.
  • New York has the largest tech talent pool in the US. It's also close to Fortune 500 enterprises in financial services, media, healthcare and retail, and its time zone overlaps with talent hubs in Europe and India.
  • Our NYC teams cover the full range of enterprise AI: AI research (reinforcement learning, information retrieval, agent evaluation), AI infrastructure like Unity Gateway, and agentic applications like CustomerLake.

When Databricks opened its New York R&D hub at 5 Bryant Park earlier this year, we made a bet: world-class AI would be built right here in Manhattan. Today, that bet is paying off.

Our NYC engineering team is already shaping the future of enterprise AI, from foundational research to the products that put AI to work for the world's largest organizations. Our NYC office is one of the largest concentrations of AI research talent in the city.

Today, we're announcing a major expansion of our NYC footprint. We're doubling our square footage at 5 Bryant Park, growing to approximately 120,000 square feet across five floors with plans to keep growing our headcount in the city. The expansion will include a dedicated Engineering and Research floor purpose-built for focused R&D work, alongside enhanced spaces for our go-to-market teams, an Executive Briefing Center, and room for significant future growth.

New York isn't just catching up to the Bay Area in tech; it's carving out its own identity as a major AI metropolis.

A recent study showed that New York City is the largest tech talent hub in the country. But what makes NYC uniquely powerful for Databricks goes beyond raw talent numbers:

  • Industry proximity - New York is the global nerve center for financial services, media, healthcare, and retail, with by far the most Fortune 500 companies headquartered here. These companies are where AI gets shaped in the real world, and where the AI rubber meets the industry road. This is where AI succeeds or fails, outside of the lab. Our engineers don't just build AI products in the abstract, they build them alongside the enterprises who deploy them.
  • A talent-rich ecosystem - With world-class institutions like Columbia, NYU, Princeton, and a thriving startup and venture capital scene, NYC produces a deep pipeline of AI and engineering talent. We've seen firsthand that top new graduates increasingly want to build their careers here, and Databricks gives them the opportunity to work on problems at the frontier of data and AI without leaving the city.
  • A global capital - New York is one of the top cities where young graduates want to work, and its time zone offers the most overlap in the US with major talent hubs in Europe and India. With Databricks teams spanning the world, New York is well positioned to connect these hubs and attract top international talent.

Our NYC teams are building the products and research that define how enterprises adopt AI. Here's a look at what's happening at 5 Bryant Park:

  • AI Research - Our research team is tackling some of the most challenging problems in enterprise AI. Our New York City office is home to our Chief AI Scientist and research teams building the technologies that power Genie and Unity Gateway, with specialities in reinforcement learning, large-scale information retrieval, and evaluating AI enterprise agents.
  • AI Infrastructure - The AI infrastructure teams work on products like Unity Gateway, which is the main AI gateway for many of the biggest enterprises in the world. At a time when AI models evolve faster than ever, Unity Gateway gives enterprises governance over cost, model and provider selection. Instead of defaulting to the most expensive LLM every time, for example, Unity Gateway can automatically route workloads to the most appropriate underlying model, helping companies optimize their AI spend and resources. Unity Gateway also offers all the necessary access and security controls to safeguard their data assets and IP.
  • AI Applications - Our NYC team is a major contributor to Lakehouse-embedded agentic vertical applications, including CustomerLake: Databricks’ next-generation agentic app for customer data and marketing.

Together, these teams span the full spectrum of cutting-edge AI, from fundamental research and infrastructure to applications for specific industries and business needs. Few companies bring such a broad range of AI expertise together at a single site.

Built on an open source foundation, the Databricks Data + AI Platform gives teams a simple way to build AI that understands their business context. From foundational research that pushes the boundaries of what's possible, to products that over 20,000 organizations such adidas, AT&T, Bayer, Bock, Mastercard, OpenAI, Rivian, Unilever and 70% of the Fortune 500 rely on every day, our NYC team is at the center of that mission.

entries.title: Transactions are Generally Available, advancing warehousing on the Lakehouse
entries.summary: Multi-Statement Transactions are Generally Available, enabling organizations to run...
entries.content:
Multi-statement transactions are Generally Available on Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg, enabling organizations to run scalable, governed, and performant warehouse workloads on the lakehouse

by Benjamin Mathew, Prakhar Jain and Sumeet Varma

Multi-Statement Transactions are Generally Available, enabling organizations to run complex, multi-step workflows with atomic guarantees without needing separate warehouse systems.

Data warehouses power some of an enterprise’s most important workloads, including data ingestion, transformation, business intelligence, applications, and operational analytics. Many of these workloads require changes across multiple tables to succeed or fail together. Historically, organizations relied on separate warehouse systems for these transactional guarantees, adding expensive data movement, duplicate copies, fragmented governance, and operational complexity.

Databricks is the first lakehouse architecture to support multi-statement transactions natively across both Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables. Alongside stored procedures, temporary tables, and SQL scripting, multi-statement transactions bring traditional data warehousing workloads to open, governed data on the lakehouse.

Traditional and cloud warehouses provide transactional guarantees, but often at the cost of a fragmented data architecture:

  • Additional copies and data movement: Moving data into and out of a separate warehouse adds latency, cost, and inconsistency risk.
  • Fragmented governance: Teams must duplicate and synchronize access policies, auditing, and operational controls across systems.
  • Complex consistency workarounds: Developers need custom orchestration, reconciliation, and retry logic to keep related changes consistent.

Multi-statement transactions bring these guarantees directly to the open, governed lakehouse, reducing duplicate systems and the operational work required to keep them aligned.

Transactions on the lakehouse provide a foundation for running demanding warehouse workloads on open enterprise data. They combine support for open table formats with unified governance and high-concurrency performance. They also integrate with familiar warehouse development tools, data pipelines, and production observability capabilities.

Open across Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg

Multi-statement transactions support both Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables. Teams can preserve open table formats while gaining atomic guarantees across multiple statements and tables. They do not have to move governed data into a proprietary format or maintain a transactional copy in another system.

Fast at high concurrency

The lakehouse architecture supports row-level concurrency, allowing concurrent transactions to write to the same table as long as they do not update the same row. Unlike traditional data warehouses, which use locks to serialize writes, row-level concurrency enables more transactions to run in parallel. As a result, Databricks delivers significantly stronger performance than traditional cloud and legacy warehouses, allowing organizations to run demanding warehouse workloads directly on the lakehouse.

Integrated with warehouse development and data pipelines

Transactions are composable with other warehousing capabilities, enabling teams to build traditional data warehousing workloads on the lakehouse. For example, developers can stage intermediate results in a temporary table, package multi-step business logic in a stored procedure, and commit the entire workflow atomically.

Transactions can also write to streaming tables, bringing atomic guarantees to workflows that continuously ingest, transform, and publish data. Now, downstream pipelines can receive consistent updates, preventing them from processing incomplete data.

Governed transactions on sensitive data

Transactions respect Unity Catalog attribute-based access controls, including row-level security and column masking, on both reads and writes. This is especially important for workflows that stage, validate, and publish sensitive data.

Observability in in production

Production transactions need to be understandable as well as correct. Developers can use commands such as 

DESCRIBE TABLE
, 
SHOW COLUMNS
, and 
GET DIAGNOSTICS
to inspect the tables involved in a transaction and capture information about transactional execution. These capabilities make transactional workflows easier to develop, operate, and troubleshoot.

This fully integrated experience enables Fivetran to build their connectors on top of lakehouse transactions.

"Fivetran History Mode preserves each version of a record using slowly changing dimensions (SCD) Type 2. Each source change is two destination writes: closing out the prior version and inserting the new active one - both must succeed together. Previously, with transactional guarantees scoped to a single statement, we ran these as separate operations and defended against partial failure with reconciliation logic and consistency checks on subsequent syncs. With multi-statement, multi-table transactions, we now commit the close and the insert as one atomic unit so either the full change is applied or none of it is. This let Fivetran remove an entire class of consistency-repair code and gave our customers a stronger correctness guarantee on historical data."—Egidio Terra, Staff Product Manager, Fivetran

Likewise, Accolade uses transactions to process thousands of claims and liabilities records every day.

"At Accolade, we process roughly 1,700 transactions in production every day to handle incoming claims and liabilities. Each of those updates has to complete reliably and consistently. Multi-statement, multi-table transactions let us run these multi-step operations with full transactional guarantees, directly on our governed lakehouse. That reliability is central to our broader migration of critical workloads to the open lakehouse, without standing up a separate warehouse."—Akshay Ajgaonkar, Engineering Manager, Accolade

Together, open formats, centralized governance, row-level concurrency, familiar SQL features, pipeline integration, and observability create a complete transactional experience on the lakehouse.

Multi-statement, multi-table transactions support several common patterns for modernizing ETL, migrating warehouse workloads, and publishing trusted data.

Give ETL multi-table transactional guarantees

An ETL job can update related tables as one unit. In this example, the order status and inventory balance cannot fall out of sync.

If either update fails, the workflow can roll back both changes rather than publishing a fulfilled order without the corresponding inventory adjustment.

Migrate warehouse procedures to the lakehouse

Stored procedures and temporary tables let developers preserve familiar warehouse development patterns while operating on governed lakehouse data.

Unity Catalog row-level security and column masking policies continue to apply to governed reads and writes. The procedure also uses 

DESCRIBE TABLE
to inspect the target’s schema and metadata before the next set of writes, helping developers verify its configuration and troubleshoot issues without leaving the transactional workflow.

Implement Write-Audit-Publish

Write-Audit-Publish prevents data from becoming visible until it passes the required quality checks.

The workflow stages new data, records its quality results, and publishes the validated records in one atomic operation. If a validation or write fails, the transaction can roll back instead of exposing a partial result. The same pattern can include transactional writes to streaming tables when downstream pipelines need the published data continuously.

Multi-Statement Transactions are Generally Available for UC managed Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables on Databricks. Get started with transactions today using Databricks’s documentation or by prompting the in-product Assistant.

With transactions on the lakehouse, you can bring critical warehouse workloads to open, governed data while reducing duplicate systems, data movement, and operational complexity.

entries.title: Closing the Binary Blind Spot: Domain-Knowledge Injection for LLM Malware Triage in npm Packages
entries.summary: IntroductionSupply chain attacks on package registries have grown in volume and sophistication [1]...
entries.content:
Supply chain attacks on package registries have grown in volume and sophistication [1]. Public research regularly observes malware being deployed to the npm registry by a range of threat actors, from spam campaigns [2] to the steady proliferation of DPRK malware [3, 4, 5], and to the high-impact TeamPCP in 2025 and 2026 [6, 7], with the DPRK and TeamPCP actors having a track record of successfully compromising widely used open source projects for maximized downstream reach [8].

To study this problem directly, we have been collecting npm malware samples since November 2025, and observed that, among the 11,413 package-versions we scanned and corroborated through OSV npm malware advisories [9], most malware on the npm registry hides its payload in the package source or fetches it from an external server, accounting for 96.2% of the corroborated dataset. The remaining 3.8%, 432 package-versions, bundle a binary. Though small in volume, they can carry disproportionate risk during triage. A stripped, opaque binary that carries no source for tools to read can be nested within a facade of clean source and metadata and potentially skew an LLM towards a benign verdict.

We evaluate how a panel of LLMs reason over crafted binary payloads at varying obfuscation and ambiguity, identify the failure modes specific to this vector, and close them with a purpose-built, cost-effective encoding of domain knowledge that improves detection quality for both budget and frontier models alike.

To support the wider research community, we built a scanner that monitors the npm registry in real time and runs a static stage before LLM triage, with YARA [10] on the tarball, Semgrep [11] and the npm registry API on the JavaScript and metadata, and a binary-analysis module over the compiled artifact. It assembles the output into a structured prompt, and the LLM returns a verdict with reasoning, requesting additional files over up to three rounds.

Our analysis found packages with bundled binaries to be both the rarest and the hardest for the pipeline to triage. An adversary distributing malicious JavaScript can assume the target already has the runtime to execute the payload, whereas a binary must be compiled for a range of target machines. Across OSV-confirmed npm malware, binary-bearing packages fail to reach a decisive malicious verdict more than twice as often as source-only ones (14.4% vs 6.2%).

Prior work instruction-tunes open-source models on expert-authored data, baking the knowledge into the weights [12]. That route cannot reach the closed, hosted models, and it requires retraining as the threat landscape shifts. We take the opposite approach and supply the expertise at inference, as pre-computed static evidence placed in the prompt before the model reasons.

We evaluate whether LLMs can detect malicious logic concealed within precompiled binaries in otherwise clean packages. A secondary question is whether the detection failures are systematic rather than random. Third, whether encoding domain knowledge of the binary problem can improve detection accuracy.

We built five payload types (Table 1) of native Node.js addons (.node files) covering common supply chain attack patterns. Imports range from defensible (fopen, connect, gethostname) to rarely legitimate (execve with dup2), and each package wraps the binary in a professional package.json, README, JavaScript bindings, and binding.gyp.

The sysmon stealer spans an obfuscation ladder from a readable baseline to a hardened build with symbols stripped and strings XOR-encoded, while the other four types appear at a single obfuscation level. We chose single-byte XOR deliberately, since unlike a stronger cipher such as RC4 it leaves no structural markers in disassembly for a model to catch.

The set mirrors collected malware. Across the OSV-confirmed npm packages shipping a binary, formats are PE, ELF (all stripped), and Mach-O, with behaviors spanning credential and environment theft, persistence, exfiltration and C2, host reconnaissance, and droppers.

Table 1. Adversarial payload types and their import profiles.

Package Type Key Imports Ambiguity
sysmon-native Credential stealer fopen, connect, send, gethostname HIGH
buildchain-native Dropper/backdoor execve, connect, chmod, socket, fwrite LOW
netpulse-native Reverse shell execve, dup2, connect, socket LOW
hashworker-native Cryptominer stub pthread_create, connect, send, recv MEDIUM
taskd-native Persistence system, fopen, fwrite, chmod MEDIUM

We evaluated nine models across seven providers (Table 2): seven budget models a team would realistically run across its codebase, four of them open-weight, and two higher-capability baselines as behavioral baseline references at higher price points. We also ran Claude Opus 4.6, the most expensive model, only as a cost reference.

Table 2. Models evaluated and their roles.

Model Provider Role Type
Claude Haiku 4.5 Anthropic Budget Proprietary
Google Gemini 3.5 Flash Budget Proprietary
Gemma 3 12B Budget Open-weight
GPT-5.4-nano OpenAI Budget Proprietary
Qwen3-Next 80B Alibaba Budget Open-weight
GLM 5.3 Flash Zhipu Budget Open-weight
Llama 3.1 8B Meta Budget Open-weight
Claude Sonnet 4.6 Anthropic Baseline behavior Proprietary
Kimi K3 Moonshot Baseline behavior Open-weight
Claude Opus 4.6 Anthropic Cost baseline Proprietary

To isolate the profiles, each payload was scanned twice per model, once without profiles and once with them. Prompt, context, and binary analysis were identical across both runs. Inference settings were held constant across every model and both conditions: temperature 0, the same system and analysis prompts throughout, and an 8192-token output cap.

A capability profile is a declarative playbook that encodes one malicious technique, such as credential harvesting or persistence, as a set of weighted conditions over the scanner's static evidence. The profiles cover source and binary techniques across npm and PyPI.

Figure 1 shows how a profile enters a scan:

  • The static stage extracts evidence from the package.
  • Each profile scores that evidence against its suspicious, malicious, and critical thresholds, a scale separate from the model's own verdict.
  • When a threshold is reached, the engine injects a structured summary (~1,800 tokens) into the prompt before the model reasons, along with any findings from the static and metadata analyzer stage.
  • The model forms its own verdict over the combined evidence and, in this experiment, may override a firing profile entirely.

Figure 1. The scan pipeline with capability profiles.

Each model was scanned against all ten payloads. We count HIGHLY_SUSPICIOUS or MALICIOUS as a detection success; SUSPICIOUS or BENIGN on a known-malicious payload is a failure. The failure analysis centers on the seven-model budget tier (70 model-payload tests); the two baselines (20 tests) serve only as a reference ceiling and are reported separately.

Without profiles, the budget tier failed on 35 of 70 tests (50%), 20 of them outright benign, and fell short of the malicious bar on 51 (73%). The two behavior baselines failed none at the escalation threshold and fell short of malicious only once (Sonnet, sysmon v3). Within the budget tier the failures followed distinct, repeatable model-specific patterns (Table 3) rather than random error; Gemini alone matched the baselines on detection, though through confabulated reasoning rather than genuine analysis. The full verdict and confidence matrix is in the appendix (Table A1).

With profiles enabled, 32 of the 35 no-profile detection failures (91%) recover to a detection, and no model returns a benign verdict on any payload. Every model that failed without profiles reached full detection with them, except GPT-5.4-nano, whose three residual failures stay at suspicious on three payloads. Across the affordable tier, failures at the escalation threshold fell from 50% to 4% (3 of 70), and at the malicious bar from 73% to 34%.

Table 3. Per-model detection rate (verdict at highly suspicious or above on a known-malicious payload) without and with capability profiles.

Model Without profiles With profiles
GPT-5.4-nano 0/10 7/10
Qwen3-Next 80B 1/10 10/10
Llama 3.1 8B 4/10 10/10
Gemma 3 12B 5/10 10/10
Claude Haiku 4.5 6/10 10/10
GLM 5.3 Flash 9/10 10/10
Gemini 3.5 Flash 10/10 10/10
Claude Sonnet 4.6 10/10 10/10
Kimi K3 10/10 10/10

The clearest single case is Qwen3-Next on the obfuscated sysmon-native stealer: benign at 0.98 recommending allowlist without profiles, malicious at 0.98 recommending block with them, on byte-identical input, after four profiles fired. The baselines, Sonnet and Kimi, were already correct without profiles, and the evidence strengthens their verdicts, so the profiles reinforce rather than distort a model that already reasons correctly.

Technique-specific profiles fired according to each payload’s attack pattern.

Table 4. Capability profiles triggered per payload at critical or malicious threshold.

Package Critical Profiles Triggered
sysmon-native T004 (Binary Masquerade), T001 (Credential Harvesting), T002 (Network Exfiltration), T003 (Environment Reconnaissance)
buildchain-native T004 (Binary Masquerade), T007 (Dropper/Stager), T002 (Network Exfiltration), T001 (Credential Harvesting)
netpulse-native T004 (Binary Masquerade), T006 (Reverse Shell)
hashworker-native T004 (Binary Masquerade), T002 (Network Exfiltration)
taskd-native T004 (Binary Masquerade)

The experiment surfaced four failure modes, each spanning a large fraction of the panel rather than any single model (Table 5). They are not mutually exclusive, since one benign verdict can be both a dismissal and a rationalization, so the table reports per-mode prevalence and a model's row can sum past ten. We read dismissal and hedging from the verdict tier, rationalization and confabulation from the written reasoning.

Two factors explain them. The first is domain knowledge, which budget LLMs lack for interpreting binary structural evidence in a package's context [13]. The second is raw capability. Reading a stripped, string-obfuscated binary requires disassembly and decoding that the budget tier did not attempt.

Table 5. Per-model failure-mode counts across the ten payloads without profiles, spanning all nine models (90 scans).

Model Rationalization Dismissal Hedging Confabulation
Haiku 4.5 4 – 4 4
Sonnet 4.6 – – – 4
Gemini 3.5 Flash – – – 4
Gemma 3 12B 5 5 – –
GLM 5.3 Flash 1 – 1 2
GPT-5.4-nano 10 2 8 –
Kimi K3 – – – 6
Qwen3-Next 80B 9 9 – –
Llama 3.1 8B 5 4 2 1
Models (of 9) 6 4 4 6
Prevalence ~37% 22% 16% ~23%

An ensemble that takes the majority verdict would not resolve this. On the obfuscated sysmon-native stealer (version 2), the nine verdicts split three benign (Gemma, Qwen, Llama), two suspicious (Haiku, GPT-5.4-nano), one highly suspicious (GLM), three malicious (Gemini, Kimi, Sonnet): the majority sits below the detection threshold, so the vote returns the wrong answer. The modes do not cancel out; they compound, so no voting scheme gives reliable coverage without first closing the domain-knowledge gap. This matches known limits of majority voting in LLM ensembles, where correlated errors converge on the wrong answer rather than canceling [14, 15].

Rationalization (~37% of scans, six models) invokes contextual cues, the install script, native-module packaging, or package description, to build a benign interpretation that overrides the binary signals. Haiku called the unobfuscated sysmon v1 MALICIOUS 0.98, but once the strings were XOR-encoded its verdict fell to SUSPICIOUS, treating node-gyp-build as standard and the .node extension as a legitimate addon, matching documented post-hoc rationalization [16]. Obfuscation thus inverts the expected relationship. The more thoroughly the payload is concealed, the lower the assigned severity, and because the rationale stays internally coherent, evaluation on unobfuscated samples would never elicit it.

Dismissal (22%, four models) returns a benign verdict without engaging the binary at all. Qwen3-Next returned BENIGN 0.98 on nine of the ten payloads and recommended allowlisting each, including the netpulse reverse shell and the taskd persistence tool, with a stated intent that ignored the binary's imports entirely. The verdict is insensitive to import ambiguity, and the uniform high confidence conceals the failure from any downstream threshold.

Hedging (16%, four models) registers suspicion but never escalates to a decisive verdict. GPT-5.4-nano returned SUSPICIOUS at 0.55-0.62 on eight of the ten payloads, never reaching highly suspicious or malicious, with buildchain-native drawing only SUSPICIOUS 0.62 and a recommended action of "Monitor." A suspicious verdict looks like functioning analysis while adding nothing beyond the YARA and Semgrep stages, and under a policy that blocks only at the malicious threshold these payloads pass.

Confabulation (~23%, six models) is the odd case, where the verdict is correct but its justification is fabricated, so a pipeline that logs it for audit accumulates fabricated indicators that mislead a later analyst or any model fine-tuned on them. It appears even in both baselines, so it recurs regardless of capability tier. Gemini is the clearest case. It returned MALICIOUS on all ten payloads but invented the detail, reporting "a decryption routine at address 0x401490" on taskd and "a custom XOR decryption loop at 0x4013b0" on netpulse, though neither address exists in the scan input and neither payload contains a cipher. The fabrication concentrates where the evidence is thinnest, in the single-function x86 payloads whose scan exposes one real address.

The under-detections are structural, not a defect of individual models. The budget-tier failures below the escalation threshold are dominated by rationalization and dismissal, where the binary sits alongside clean source, a node-gyp-build install script, professional metadata, and a plausible README, each unremarkable for a native module. No single artifact misleads the model. Every one of the 35 failures leans on at least two of these benign signals, 24 on four at once, and 14 recast the binary's own imports as standard system calls (Table 6). LLMs can analyze binary evidence in isolation [17, 18], but here the failure is contextual.

Table 6. Benign contextual signals cited across the 35 detection failures.

Benign Signal Cited Count
install script (node-gyp-build) called standard 35/35
native-addon / .node packaging 35/35
metadata / stated purpose "consistent with" 32/35
clean lib/index.js JavaScript 21/35
binary's own imports recast as "standard/normal" 14/35

The modes are predictable in that each model exhibits one, though none is deterministic across a model's whole output, so defenders cannot simply pick a better model. The two categories even fail differently, with dismissal almost entirely an open-weight behavior (18 of the 20 no-profile benign verdicts from Gemma, Qwen, and Llama) while the proprietary models rarely dismiss and instead rationalize, hedge, or confabulate. This bears on model selection. A test set of a few unobfuscated or low-ambiguity packages makes a budget model look sufficient while hiding its failure on the obfuscated credential stealer, and obfuscation recurs in real malware, with the Binary String Obfuscation profile firing on 74 of the 425 OSV-confirmed binary packages (17%). Testing only high-ambiguity payloads has the opposite effect, condemning a serviceable model and pushing a team to overspend on a frontier one. A correct verdict also does not imply a correct label, as budget models often flagged maliciousness while assigning the wrong category, so the category and stated evidence are triage hints, not ground truth for attribution.

The baselines Sonnet 4.6 and Kimi K3 detected every payload without profiles, at roughly 3x the per-scan cost of the budget tier, which with profiles matches that accuracy at the lower price. Profiles also change the token work each model does (Table 7), and the direction depends on how hard the model works unaided. The budget tier takes a modest input premium from the ~1,800-token evidence block, with input rising 9 to 34% and its analysis otherwise unchanged, whereas the thorough models move the other way. Opus, which without profiles gathers about 10.5K input tokens per scan requesting extra files, drops to 7.2K with them (−32%), and Kimi emits 13% fewer output tokens for the same reason. Profiles add a small, bounded input cost to the cheap models and claw back far more from the expensive ones.

Table 7. Per-model token usage per scan, averaged over the ten payloads, without and with capability profiles.

Model Input (no profiles) Input (profiles) Δ input Output (no profiles) Output (profiles) Δ output
Haiku 4.5 5,381 7,213 +34% 933 1,616 +73%
Gemini 3.5 Flash 7,000 7,614 +9% 493 488 −1%
Gemma 3 12B 5,866 7,623 +30% 420 506 +21%
GPT-5.4-nano 4,900 6,428 +31% 568 729 +28%
Qwen3-Next 80B 5,691 7,267 +28% 523 772 +48%
GLM 5.3 Flash 5,531 6,606 +19% 746 1,110 +49%
Llama 3.1 8B 4,884 6,402 +31% 302 351 +16%
Sonnet 4.6 5,382 7,214 +34% 1,150 1,472 +28%
Kimi K3 8,706 9,388 +8% 5,572 4,842 −13%
Opus 4.6 10,551 7,214 −32% 1,254 1,370 +9%

Public OSV advisories [9], excluding withdrawn entries, confirm 470 malicious npm package-versions that ship a native binary, 604 binaries in total. By format they are PE (273), ELF (215, every one stripped), and Mach-O (113), with 3 unidentified; by compiler, 363 are native C or C++, 183 Go, and 58 Rust. The 241 Go or Rust binaries, 40% of the total, are the case the engine's runtime-aware gating exists for, and 50, all ELF, are UPX-packed. Of these 470, 425 fall in our scanned, non-withdrawn corpus form the evaluation set in Detection.

The benign set is defined from external signals only, with no reliance on the engine's own verdict. A package qualifies when it ships a native binary, exceeds one million monthly downloads, and has never appeared in OSV, giving 2,449 package-versions across 287 distinct packages. The scanner escalates 104 of them to highly suspicious or above, a false-positive rate of 4.25% of package-versions, concentrated in 6 distinct packages, 2% of the 287. On all 104 the static playbooks also fired, and on 33 a binary capability profile reached the malicious or critical threshold, so the escalation reflected genuine signals in the binary, packing, high-entropy sections, and suspicious imports. The residual false-positive rate is a property of static binary ambiguity.

The evaluation set is the 425 binary-bearing package-versions from the Malicious Set that carry a production verdict (the non-withdrawn subset in our verdicted corpus). Against these and the benign set, the scanner reaches precision 0.77, recall 0.81, and F1 0.79 at the escalation threshold (Table 8). Recall is scored against OSV's package-level label, which does not isolate the malicious artifact, and a binary capability profile drove 74% of the detections while the rest were escalated on JavaScript, metadata, or source signals.

Table 8. Detection performance across OSV-confirmed binary malware and the benign validation corpus at the escalation threshold.

TP FN FP TN Precision Recall F1
345 80 104 2345 0.77 0.81 0.79

The scanner recovers 345 of the 425 positives; 60 fall to suspicious and 20 are cleared as benign, a 4.7% hard-miss rate. Inspecting the metadata of the 20 cleared packages, without opening the binaries, about half bundle a recognizable third-party tool unchanged (ripgrep, node-pty, NSIS installer plugins) where OSV attributes the malice to the install or JavaScript layer; the rest ship the package's own compiled CLI, flagged for an account-compromise campaign or a low-confidence advisory. The binary-level miss rate is thus lower than the headline, though we do not claim every cleared binary is benign.

The production figures are measured against OSV's package-level labels, which mark a whole package malicious without isolating the responsible artifact; some cleared packages are mislabeled, their payload in JavaScript or metadata rather than the binary. So the reported recall and false-positive rate describe performance against those labels, not binary detection specifically, which could be somewhat higher or lower. And the hosted models sit behind continuously updated endpoints, so absolute verdicts reflect one serving epoch and may drift, which is why our conclusions rest on the within-epoch delta between no-profile and with-profile conditions on byte-identical inputs, not on any single verdict.

The four failure modes, rationalization, dismissal, hedging, and confabulation, recur across the panel, producing detection failures on 50% of budget-tier tests at the escalation threshold and 73% at the stricter malicious bar. Capability profiles, which inject pre-computed binary domain knowledge before the model reasons, cut escalation-threshold failures to 4% and eliminate every benign verdict, while holding false positives on the benign set to 4.25% of package-versions (104 of 2,449; 2% of distinct packages), low enough for an analyst to clear by hand. Together these let a far cheaper model match the detection accuracy of a substantially more expensive one.

entries.summary: At Databricks, we continuously develop and evaluate new AI research techniques to...
entries.content:
by Ethan Tang, Ivan Zhou, Irene Dea, Steven Chen, Bruce Fontaine and Ben Hansen

  • Databricks AI Research uses AI Runtime to train and fine-tune models at scale, from small experiments to workloads spanning hundreds of GPUs.
  • Built-in GPU reliability, fast job launches, and integrations with MLflow and Unity Catalog help researchers experiment faster.
  • Agent-driven research has increased training jobs 8x, with AI Runtime supporting faster, automated experimentation.

At Databricks, we continuously develop and evaluate new AI research techniques to make our products more intelligent, efficient, and useful for customers.

Our research spans products like Genie, Smart Routing, and AI Functions. Recently, we've published how we made search 3x faster, developed new techniques for offline reinforcement learning, and pushed the frontier of complex document extraction.

To build great AI models and manage hundreds of parallel research workstreams, we need infrastructure that can keep pace. That's why we use Databricks AI Runtime (AIR).

In this post, we'll share how AIR helps us experiment quickly, scale to large training workloads, and adapt to agent-led training, along with what we've learned about managing GPU resources across research projects.

Our research team develops models that power Databricks AI Functions, including 

ai_parse_document
and 
ai_extract
. For example, Databricks AI Functions deliver state-of-the-art document parsing quality, backed by models trained to understand enterprise documents. Achieving that quality requires extensive research across different architectures, datasets, training techniques, and hyperparameters, spanning tens of thousands of training and evaluation runs.

We use supervised fine-tuning (SFT), offline reinforcement learning (RL), and online RL to train models ranging from a few billion parameters to nearly a trillion. Depending on the workload, we use NVIDIA H100 or B300 GPUs, both available through AIR. Our largest training runs can require hundreds of GPUs working together over days or weeks, with high-bandwidth networking to keep training efficient.

Supporting these workloads creates three challenges:

  • Resiliency for long-running training jobs. Training can require thousands of GPU hours. A single node or RDMA network failure can leave hundreds of GPUs idle and force us to restart from an earlier checkpoint, losing hours of progress. For reinforcement learning projects like KARL, reliable infrastructure is essential.
  • Fast experimentation and prototyping. Improving AI Functions means testing thousands of approaches, from different models and training techniques to data recipes. We need to launch experiments quickly without repeatedly provisioning infrastructure or rebuilding environments.
  • GPU fleet management. We balance multiple research projects with different compute requirements, priorities, and deadlines, while remaining flexible enough to respond to new research techniques or open-source models.

Our research team has been customer zero of AI Runtime since the product's inception last year. We use AIR to develop, train, and test models that power Databricks AI products, relying on its GPU infrastructure and integration with our existing tools.

Built-in GPU resiliency

AIR performs preflight checks on assigned GPU nodes to ensure they're healthy and can communicate effectively before training starts. It also monitors node health during execution, detecting issues such as NCCL communication failures, thermal or power throttling, and GPU driver problems. If a node becomes unhealthy and causes a job to fail, AIR detects the issue and cordons off the affected node so subsequent jobs aren't scheduled on the same problematic infrastructure.

This is especially important for projects like KARL, where complex rollout generation and post-training of models with more than 100 billion parameters can require thousands of GPU hours. Rather than repeatedly troubleshooting infrastructure failures, we can focus on improving our models.

Fast iteration with the AIR CLI and custom containers

Research requires us to change model configurations, training approaches, and code frequently. With the AIR CLI, we can launch workloads programmatically, specify the GPUs we need, and let AIR handle provisioning and scheduling, including high-bandwidth networking for distributed training across clouds.

We also rely on custom Docker containers for local development. AIR lets us use those same images for training, ensuring compatibility without recreating our environments. We can upload our codebase, execute custom code in those containers, and use Databricks Artifact Registry to register and share images across experiments. AIR's investments in launch latency and container optimization help us start training jobs in seconds, shortening feedback loops as we test new ideas.

MLflow and logging for experiment tracking

We use MLflow to track our research experiments. AIR automatically creates and manages MLflow experiments for our training jobs, eliminating separate configuration.

We can monitor job status, stream and inspect training logs, and retrieve metrics to understand how experiments are progressing. This also gives our AI agents access to the information they need to evaluate results and determine what to try next.

Seamless, governed access to research data

All of our research data is stored in Unity Catalog. Through Unity Catalog FUSE mounting, AIR lets us access that data as though it were part of a local filesystem, even when working across different Databricks workspaces.

This keeps our data accessible, tracked, shareable, and governed without changing how our training code interacts with files. Combined with MLflow and our Docker-based environments, it gives us a consistent workflow from local development to distributed training.

Managing GPU capacity across research projects

Our workloads have very different resource needs. A debugging experiment may require only a few GPUs, while a large training run might need hundreds for days or weeks. Different projects also have competing timelines and priorities.

AIR's workload prioritization and preemption capabilities help us allocate resources across projects, prioritize time-sensitive experiments, and use excess capacity when it's available. For example, spare capacity can support additional exploratory experiments over a weekend without disrupting higher-priority work. Our goal is to keep GPU resources available for the experiments that matter, without requiring researchers to manually coordinate infrastructure.

Popularized by Andrej Karpathy, autoresearch is changing how we develop AI models. Instead of researchers manually launching and evaluating every experiment, we're increasingly using agents to propose changes, run experiments, evaluate results, and determine what to try next.

This shift has dramatically increased our experimentation volume. Across our AI Functions research workloads, the number of training jobs has grown by 8x.

As agents take on more of the research process, our infrastructure needs to keep up. A slow startup or confusing configuration error might be manageable when a researcher launches a handful of experiments. When agents launch hundreds, those same issues quickly become bottlenecks.

Agent-driven research requires fast job launches, programmatic interfaces, clear and actionable errors, reliable execution, and accessible training results.

Our autoresearch workflow follows a continuous cycle:

  • Propose: Agents identify potential improvements to models or training approaches.
  • Launch trials: They submit multiple experiments to AIR in parallel.
  • Learn: They evaluate training metrics to identify what improves performance.
  • Update the plan: They use the results to refine their approach and launch new experiments.

AIR is particularly well suited to this workflow because agents can interact with it programmatically and benefit from its fast job launches, built-in reliability, and ability to scale. Through the Databricks CLI and 

databricks-air-skills
, our agents can launch concurrent workloads, monitor job status, retrieve MLflow metrics, and iterate based on the results.

This lets us run more experiments while our researchers focus on developing new ideas and improving model quality. As we move further toward agent-driven research, AIR gives us the infrastructure to support both larger models and a faster pace of experimentation.

Our experience using AI Runtime has shown us how much reliable, flexible GPU infrastructure matters for research. From large-scale training and governed data access to agent-driven experimentation, AIR lets us spend less time managing infrastructure and more time developing better models.

If you're training or fine-tuning your own models, check out the AI Runtime documentation to get started.

AI Runtime has also powered our research across areas like faster search, reinforcement learning, and document understanding. Explore more of our work at Databricks AI Research,

entries.content:
The same Stripe pipeline that feeds your lakehouse analytics can now power your applications

by Carlota Soto

  • Stripe Data Pipeline now streams real-time Stripe data directly into Databricks Lakebase Postgres — no code required.
  • Eliminates the need to build and maintain custom API or webhook integrations to keep Stripe data in sync with your app.
  • Apps can gate features, show live billing details, and trigger personalized offers using simple SQL against always-current Stripe data.

If your business runs on Stripe, your application needs access to Stripe data at runtime to respond to customer activity, whether that's confirming a payment, updating subscription access, or displaying billing details. Keeping that data in sync with Stripe has traditionally meant building and maintaining custom integrations with APIs or webhooks.

That's changing. Stripe Data Pipeline now supports real-time sync to Postgres [link Stripe's blog post], and Databricks Lakebase is one of the supported destinations (blog and documentation) powered by OpenSharing. Stripe streams real-time API data into Lakebase and manages the sync end to end.

Earlier this year, Stripe data became available to sync to Databricks through Stripe Data Pipeline. With real-time sync to Postgres, one Stripe account can now feed two Databricks destinations, each built for a different kind of work.

Stripe shares your payments, customers, subscriptions, refunds, and payouts data with your workspace through Delta Sharing, so your Stripe data becomes just another table in Unity Catalog, governed and ready to join with the rest of your business data.

Teams use it to score which customers are likely to churn, ask Genie for MRR by geography, reconcile payments at month-end, and give finance teams governed apps to explore payment data. These workloads look at patterns across thousands of customers and many weeks of history.

With Stripe Data Pipeline's real-time sync to Postgres, your payment, customer, subscription, and other Stripe data is continuously synced to Lakebase, with updates arriving within seconds.

Your application can query this data to drive its logic, determining what actions to take and what content to surface based on an up-to-date view of Stripe data.

Keeping your application's database up to date with real-time Stripe data takes ongoing effort. Today, most teams rely on one of two approaches:

  • Calling the Stripe API: This works at lower volumes, but it gets harder to operate as traffic grows and rate limits come into play.
  • Webhooks: Every event needs a handler, plus retry logic for failed deliveries and a reconciliation process for events that are missed or arrive out of order.

Either way, it's a separate piece of infrastructure to build, monitor, and maintain. And when it fails, customers end up with the wrong access or outdated account details.

That infrastructure work goes away with Stripe Data Pipeline. Choose which Stripe tables to sync to Lakebase, and Stripe handles the backfill, ongoing delivery, and data audits through its no-code pipeline, helping keep your data complete and up to date.

With real-time Stripe data in Lakebase, your application can access the latest payment and subscription information to support core product functionality and customer experiences, including:

When a customer upgrades their plan, their new subscription details are reflected in Lakebase within seconds, and your application unlocks premium features on their next request. When a subscription is canceled or a renewal fails, access changes just as quickly, with no event handler in between and no window where a paying customer is stuck on the free plan.

Customers expect their account page to reflect what just happened: the plan they're on, the invoice that was paid this morning, the card that needs updating. With subscriptions, invoices, and payment data synced to Lakebase, your application can show accurate billing details wherever customers manage their account, without calling the Stripe API on every page load.

With charges, refunds, and payouts syncing continuously, you can build dashboards that show daily sales volume, payouts, and refunds as they happen.

With subscription and payment history right in your application database, you can serve contextual offers at the right moment: a win-back discount shortly after a customer cancels, an upgrade prompt when usage outgrows their plan, or a reminder when a payment method is about to expire.

Real-time sync to Postgres for Stripe Data Pipeline is available in public preview, and it's free to get started. Create a pipeline in the Stripe Dashboard and read the documentation to learn more.

Lakebase is Databricks' serverless Postgres database, built for applications and AI agents and integrated with the rest of the Databricks Data + AI Platform. Get started for free.
