entries.title: Reducing the noise: How Atlassian built an OCSF security lakehouse on Databricks
entries.summary: The challenge: Two decades of logging noise at global scaleAtlassian is a global...
entries.content:
Facing 44 billion events a day, Atlassian standardized security logs on the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and built a self-service security lakehouse on Databricks — cutting ingestion costs and powering 500+ threat-detection signals.

by Taylor Kain, Zachary Schmerber (Atlassian) and Niels Heijmans (Atlassian)

  • 80% reduction in ingestion cost after standardizing security telemetry on OCSF
  • 500+ production threat-detection signals running on a single, unified schema
  • 60% increase in analyst productivity — one repeatable process across every tool
  • Up to 95% faster queries (from ~45 seconds to 2–3 seconds) using OCSF structure
  • 44 billion events per day normalized into a common schema
  • Winner of the Databricks 2026 Transformation Award

Atlassian is a global SaaS provider serving 350,000 customers — the product of 20 years of growth and a long list of acquisitions, each of which arrived with its own logging formats. The result was a security data pipeline absorbing 44 billion events per day with no common language across various log sources.

"You've got varied timestamps, you've got proprietary schemas, you've got operational drain for anyone trying to organize and structure this information," explained Zachary Schmerber, Senior Security Logging Engineer at Atlassian and a maintainer of the OCSF schema. Analysts were burning time normalizing data after it landed, cross-platform correlation was limited because data lived in different places and shapes, and SIEM pipelines were not keeping pace.

The team needed a way to coalesce fragmented telemetry into one place and make sense of it, while maintaining flexibility and avoiding vendor lock-in.

Atlassian's answer was to standardize everything on the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and build the lakehouse on Databricks.

OCSF won because it was the only option the team considered wholly open. Compared to alternatives like ECS or UDM, it offered a strongly typed schema with robust validation that minimized ambiguity after transformation, good compression efficiency, extensibility, and an open-source community (with Linux Foundation backing and a path toward international standardization). Its roughly 40,000 fields looked daunting at first — but that verbosity turned out to be the platform's greatest asset, because the semantic context stays with the data.

"Investigations where a single query could hit many different data sources — because the data is structured," said Schmerber. "Maybe you've got five vulnerability scanners in your system. Now you have one data set instead of five."

Databricks was the natural platform. Native ACID transactions made it far easier to migrate across schema versions without breaking downstream consumers; auto-scaling Spark clusters handled shared, high-volume workloads; and the platform was built to manage the infrastructure overhead of a large, multi-team organization. Atlassian deliberately chose ETL over ELT — transforming data in flight — to enable real-time detection, preserve vendor independence, and compress data as it moved through the pipeline.

Table optimization delivered dramatic performance gains. With structured OCSF data, partitioning and Z-ORDER took a representative query from ~45 seconds to 2–3 seconds — a 95% improvement, with similar gains on larger queries. Enabling Graviton clusters with Photon cut query cost and runtime by roughly two-thirds.

A defining engineering decision was embedding the entire OCSF schema into Go structs — what the team calls "TypeGo." Because the schema lives in the type system, correctness is guaranteed at compile time.

"Every time you produce a new OCSF log, it's pre-validated — because it can't be anything but OCSF," said Schmerber. Nested objects are native, deployments can run anywhere, and everything is unit tested. Crucially, this type safety also tamed AI: when the team automated transformation with an agentic workflow, the rigid schema sharply reduced hallucinations and cut token usage, because the agent couldn't produce invalid mappings and cycle through bad iterations.

The biggest transformation was operational. Atlassian's security data-engineering team started with a six-phase manual procedure to collect logs, transform them into TypeGo, route, test, configure, and ship them via PR. Over time they automated nearly all of it — and eventually handed it back to the customer as a self-service platform.

Now an analyst identifies the logs they want and provides a canonical dataset. After a gated confirmation, the workflow scans the framework inside the Go structs, generates the mappings and the DAG, tests them locally, deploys a canary configuration via PR, validates at scale in a canary environment, and — after a soak — gets promoted to production and notifies the user of any errors. Regression testing gates everything before production.

The tool chain includes a schema-mapping IDE and an open-source Go OCSF library with validation performance enhancements, automatic handling of unmapped fields, schema helpers (IP path, normalization), and intelligent routing. The payoff is low onboarding overhead: "I can now have a SOC analyst do principal data engineer work in a production environment," said Schmerber — with every change still reviewed.

The acceleration is stark: "It took me a year to map about one-third of the data we have mapped today," Schmerber noted, "and two months to map the other two-thirds."

For the detection and response team, standardization changed how alerts get written. "Adopting the OCSF schema has enabled us to transform our threat detection pipeline by moving from one-to-one alerts to a signal- and risk-based detection methodology, where multiple signal findings are clustered together in a single alert," said Jordan of Atlassian's Detection and Response team.

Using a custom tool called Alert Explorer, findings cluster around standardized OCSF values — for example, a single 

actor.user
value that is identical whether it appears in an authentication event or a network event. That consistency lets the team standardize clustering, enrichment, and triage plays: instead of per-detection enrichment, they call an enrichment API on a standardized username value every time.

"OCSF has made it much easier to write detections and provide more meaningful, actionable alerts," said Jordan, "which analysts can dive deep into regardless of where the data came from."

Beyond the headline cost and performance numbers, standardization unlocked capabilities that were previously impractical: multi-domain correlation with strong entity resolution, efficient user-behavior analytics, and cross-application pattern analysis. With everything speaking one language, the team could write simple queries to spot anomalous behavior across five different routers — or five vulnerability scanners — at once. Dashboards were simplified dramatically because OCSF classes share objects, and storage was optimized because the team knew what data to keep and what to drop.

Schmerber is most excited about what the semantically rich schema unlocks for AI. "How do you talk to your data unless your agent has context? It'll hallucinate and give you the wrong answer," he said. Because OCSF carries its definitions inside the schema, agentic assistance becomes far more accurate.

The roadmap includes skills training that feeds an analyst's real field usage into reusable agent skills, an orchestration of agents that can run threat hunts with the right context, contextual SQL that can answer questions like "where's my DNS C2 traffic in this schema?", and context graphs built on OCSF. The longer-term ambition is semantic: making OCSF the canonical starting point that everything emits — rather than a model coalesced from data after the fact. The team will also continue with improving query performance by looking at a move to Liquid Clustering for data partitioning across environments like corporate devices and cloud.

entries.content:
Lakehouse//RT delivers ultra low latency spatial queries at scale

by Kent Marten, Matt Slack and Kaitlin Baumgardner

  • Spatial SQL and spatial joins are now supported on Lakehouse//RT, delivering ultra low latency and high concurrency directly on your governed lakehouse data.
  • Benchmarks show Lakehouse//RT delivers 38X faster spatial query performance than a traditional data warehouse with 50 concurrent users.
  • No separate geospatial serving layer required. Spatial SQL on Lakehouse//RT combines real-time performance with open formats, Unity Catalog governance, and the full 100+ spatial function library.

Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on Lakehouse//RT and they're up to 38X faster than traditional cloud data warehouses.

Earlier this year, we brought Spatial SQL to General Availability on Databricks: this included support for the GEOMETRY data type, 100+ spatial functions, high-performance spatial joins, AI/BI maps, Delta Sharing. The GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY data types are part of the open lakehouse, available in Apache Spark, and supported in the same underlying parquet files used by Delta and Iceberg v3. Customers across insurance, agriculture, energy, telecom, retail, logistics and more have adopted it to consolidate geospatial workloads onto a single governed platform.

Organizations with both spatial OLAP workloads and real-time location-based applications want great performance and high concurrency. Many of these organizations still rely on traditional data warehouses and build out specialized architectures for spatial applications, sometimes managing a separate stack centered on PostGIS for every use case just to meet latency requirements. Separate stacks lead to more copies of data, more synchronization pipelines, and more governance overhead.

Databricks now supports 4-pillars for geospatial workloads: Lakehouse for long-running spatial OLAP workloads, Lakebase for spatial OLTP, apps, and agents, Databricks Apps for purpose-built experiences, and now the Lakehouse//RT warehouse for real-time analytics. 

This blog covers what Lakehouse//RT delivers for spatial workloads, driving up to 38X performance improvement under high concurrency.

We benchmarked Lakehouse//RT against a traditional cloud data warehouse across a suite of spatial queries using SpatialBench. By comparison, Lakehouse//RT delivers 3X faster on average, and up to 20X faster across the tested queries.

Under heavy load, the performance differences are even more significant. At 50 concurrent users, Lakehouse//RT delivers up to 38X on the queries where the traditional warehouse could keep up.

Try it for yourself: Follow the SpatialBench documentation to generate the synthetic data used in the benchmark queries from this page.

Take a look at query #8. To follow best practices, it is recommended to remove the ST_GeomFromWKB call that converts data stored as well-known binary and instead use the native GEOMETRY data types. Using the native data types allows query optimizations and file-skipping to provide the best performance.

Three takeaways:

  • Lakehouse//RT is up to 38X faster, maintaining performance with high-concurrency. Even removing the most significant query improvement; the average speed-up is over 3.5X.
  • Lakehouse//RT is up to 20X faster with single-query concurrency. Every spatial benchmark query is faster on Lakehouse//RT.
  • No query changes or new licenses required. Spatial workloads are portable on Databricks; the same spatial queries you run on SQL Serverless today can run on Lakehouse//RT with no code changes.

Spatial SQL on Databricks already serves a wide range of industries. With Lakehouse//RT, workloads can run with the real-time speed applications demand. Here are a few examples:

  • Telecom and retail: Evaluate subscriber signal health in coverage areas and assess trade-area overlap for new store sites.
  • Energy and natural resources: Intersect well locations against land leases, pipeline routes against suitability corridors, and renewable sites against terrain and infrastructure.
  • Insurance and risk: Match policies to projected storm paths and calculate insured value at risk, provide real-time forecast updates to reinsurance partners.
  • Logistics and delivery: Assign orders to the nearest service area instantly.
  • Security and observability: Correlate threat signals with geographic boundaries and serve point-in-polygon lookups to dashboards and agents at high concurrency.

Spatial SQL on Lakehouse//RT is available now in Beta. To get started:

  • Create a Lakehouse//RT real-time warehouse from the SQL Warehouses page
  • Run your existing spatial queries; no code changes needed
  • Explore the Spatial SQL documentation for the full function reference

At Data + AI Summit 2026, we introduced Lakehouse//RT, Databricks' new real-time data warehouse built to deliver millisecond query performance at massive concurrency directly on your lakehouse data. Lakehouse//RT was designed to solve a specific problem: as organizations expand data access across users, applications, dashboards, and AI agents, they need real-time responsiveness without copying data into a separate serving layer. Preview customers have seen significantly better performance overall with Lakehouse//RT vs. real-time serving layers, with latency as low as 10ms and concurrency as high as 12,000 queries per second.

Yes. Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on the Lakehouse//RT, so you can serve geospatial queries with low latency and high concurrency directly on your governed Delta and Iceberg tables. There is no need to copy data into a separate geospatial system or real-time analytics serving layer.

No. The same spatial functions and spatial joins you run on Databricks SQL Serverless today run on Lakehouse//RT with no code changes. You get the speedup by creating a Lakehouse//RT warehouse and pointing your existing queries at it.

In head-to-head benchmarks against a traditional data warehouse, Lakehouse//RT runs spatial queries up to 38X faster under heavy load. On average, benchmark queries are 3.5X faster even when you exclude the largest increase.

Spatial SQL and spatial joins are available on Lakehouse//RT in Beta. To get started, create a Lakehouse//RT warehouse from the SQL Warehouses page and run your existing spatial queries with no code changes.
